a new aspect of the role of homocysteines in the pathophysiology of vascular diseases.

the possible role of chronic mild hyperhomocteinemias in the development of inflammatory diseases.

the mild hyperhomocytinemia alters the ectonucleotide metabolism, which could be involved in the inflammatory response.

the mild hyperhomocytseinemia induced by Hcy in the levels similar to considered a risk factor to development vascular diseases, modulates the activity of ectonucleotideases, which could be involved in the pro-inflammatory status.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Hcy could induce a pro-inflammatory state, which could be a risk factor to development and/or aggravation of cardiovascular and cerebral diseases.

Hcy in concentrations considered as risk factors to the development of vascular diseases can alter ectonucleotides metabolism in lymphocytes and that this alteration could be a mechanism to the development of a pro-inflammatory status.

chronic mild hyperhomcysteinemia alters the ectonucleoside triphosphatase and ecto-5-nucleotidase expression in mesenteric nodes lymphocytes, which could be related with a pro-inflammatory state and the risk to development of vascular and cerebral diseases.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the immune response can be modulated by the ectonucleotide metabolism in lymphocytes.
the ectonucleotide hydrolysis is altered in mild hyperhomocytseinemia, which can lead to a proinflammatory status.
hyperhomocysteinemias may affect the immune system and contribute to the onset of vascular diseases.
